publishedSummary: Most of the blood is in the veins, not the arteries. That single fact makes the venous system the body's volume reservoir, explains why venous pressure is read from the neck, and underlies most of the compensations that follow blood loss.

sections.narrative:
The distribution of blood around the circulation is markedly uneven. Most of the blood volume is held in the systemic veins, which therefore act as the main vascular reservoir. The arteries, for all their pressure, contain a comparatively small share.

That reservoir role follows from a mechanical property. Veins can accommodate a substantial increase in blood volume with only a small rise in venous pressure, demonstrating high compliance and capacitance. A thin-walled, collapsible vessel changes shape before it changes tension, so it can take up volume almost without resisting. The corollary matters clinically: because venous pressure changes so little with volume, a normal venous pressure does not exclude a significant change in blood volume, and by the time venous pressure is clearly abnormal the change has usually been large.

The same compliance makes the veins a controllable reservoir rather than a passive one. Their walls contain smooth muscle, and constricting them shifts blood out of storage and toward the heart. Angiotensin II directly constricts arterioles and veins — the arteriolar action raises resistance, while the venous action mobilises stored volume, so a single mediator both defends pressure and improves filling.

Two further properties allow venous pressure to be read from the outside. There are no valves between the right atrium and the venae cavae, so right-atrial pressure waves are transmitted back into the jugular veins, making the pulsations in the neck a direct display of events in the right atrium. And because venous pressure falls with vertical height above the right atrium, the height of the visible column measures that pressure: raised high in the neck it indicates a raised right-atrial pressure, while the neck veins collapse when their intraluminal pressure falls below atmospheric pressure — which is why they are normally invisible in a healthy upright person, and why position must be specified whenever the finding is recorded.

At the level of the capillary bed, perfusion is adjusted locally by the tissue being perfused. Metabolites produced by active tissue recruit more perfused capillaries and increase local vasomotion. The signal is the by-product of activity itself, so blood flow is matched to demand without any central instruction — a tissue that works harder produces more of the metabolites that open its own supply.

Recruitment matters as much as dilatation. Not every capillary in a bed is perfused at any given moment; increasing the number that carry flow raises the surface area available for exchange and shortens diffusion distances, which improves delivery more effectively than simply speeding flow through the same channels would.

The capillary bed also participates in restoring blood volume after loss. Fluid movement across the capillary wall is governed by the balance between hydrostatic pressure pushing outward and oncotic pressure drawing inward. After haemorrhage, capillary hydrostatic pressure falls, and reduced capillary hydrostatic pressure draws interstitial fluid into the circulation, helping to restore plasma volume. This autotransfusion needs no active mechanism — the same Starling balance that normally drives filtration outward simply shifts in the opposite direction. It also accounts for a familiar clinical observation: haemoglobin concentration may be near normal immediately after acute blood loss and fall over the following hours as interstitial fluid dilutes the remaining red cells.

The microcirculation is also where prolonged shock becomes irreversible. In late refractory shock, precapillary sphincters may dilate while postcapillary venules remain constricted. Blood then enters the bed more easily than it can leave, capillary hydrostatic pressure rises, and fluid is lost into the tissues instead of being recovered — the autotransfusion mechanism runs backwards, and the pooling deepens the very hypovolaemia that caused it.

Compensation for blood loss operates on several timescales, and the slowest of them is behavioural. After haemorrhage, angiotensin II and reduced baroreceptor discharge stimulate thirst.

The two signals report different things and converge on the same response. Reduced baroreceptor discharge is the immediate consequence of a fall in arterial pressure, sensed in the carotid sinus and aortic arch and relayed to the brainstem. Angiotensin II reflects the renin–angiotensin response to reduced renal perfusion, and acts on circumventricular structures that lie outside the blood–brain barrier and can therefore sample circulating hormone directly.

Thirst matters because the faster compensations cannot replace what was lost. The baroreflex redistributes and constricts; autotransfusion borrows fluid from the interstitium; venoconstriction mobilises the venous reservoir. All of these redistribute existing volume, and none adds any. Only drinking — supported by renal conservation of what is drunk — restores the total. That is why thirst belongs with the haemodynamic reflexes rather than apart from them, and why it is one of the more reliable early symptoms of significant blood loss.
